articles.title: Stephen A Smith debriefs interview with President Trump, warns Democrats face steep challenge
articles.summary: Stephen A. Smith says President Trump was "immovable" in refusing to accept blame for GOP midterm losses during their wide-ranging White House interview.
articles.body:
ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith debriefed his White House interview with President Donald Trump during an appearance Thursday on " Hannity " and cautioned Democrats over the influence of the party's far-left flank.

Smith said the pair discussed "devastating" GOP midterm losses during a 40-minute, wide-ranging interview and criticized Trump for refusing to take blame, saying he was "immovable" on that point.

"We talked about the devastating losses in the midterms and how the GOP essentially got slaughtered," Smith told Fox News host Sean Hannity.

"I asked him, is he willing to point the finger at himself, and he was dogged … he was immovable in that regard," he added.

Trump repeatedly told Americans during his midterm blitz to vote as if he were on the ballot, but Smith said the commander in chief removed himself from that narrative during their Thursday interview.

"He said, 'I wasn't on the ballot.' I said, 'That makes absolutely no sense, Mr. President. You said, put you on a ballot. That's what you told the American people to do.' He said, 'Well, they didn't do it.' I said, 'Well, what if they did do it and that was the reason you lost,'" Smith explained.

"He refused to accept that," he continued. "His attitude is that the candidates were not that great. If it were him that was running, this would not have happened. That's his mentality."

Smith explained why he doesn't agree with Trump's perception of how the midterms played out and argued that the blue wave stems from Americans being dissatisfied with his presidency.

"I think that he is somebody that is convinced his way is what it is. I just don't agree with him," Smith said.

"I think the American people made a statement against what they were seeing from him in terms of him not having his eye on the ball and coming across as a bit detached in their eyes," he added.

Smith told Fox News that Trump also gave him pushback when discussing the impact of the Iran war and tariffs on voter sentiment and the economy. He also addressed speculation that Trump offered him the role of White House press secretary .

"That was absolutely hilarious," Smith said. "Evidently, they don't know about the life that I live and the kind of affluence that ESPN and Disney have blessed me with."

"I wouldn't take that pay cut for almost anything but the presidency," he continued. "That ain't happening. Press secretary? Please."

Smith, who has lodged criticism at both Democrats and Republicans, warned that the Democratic Party faces a challenge from its far-left side.

"I definitely think that right now, the Democrats have a challenge on their hands because clearly there's a lot of people out there that view the Democratic Party as a divided party," he said. "Now they will tell you they're a very big tent and there's room for everybody, but I think that the progressive left has shown you there isn't room for everybody."

"If you're not willing to capitulate to their desires, their wishes and their ideological beliefs 100%, then they got a problem with you," he added.

Smith called out Democrats who have declined interviews and expressed gratitude that Trump agreed to sit down with him for an interview.

"[Trump] was just very rigid and immovable in his thinking that it was blown by the people who lost and that the candidates on the Republican side simply were not good enough. It was not about him," Smith said.

"I give him credit," he continued. "I asked a question, and he answered, and he didn't run from anything."

images.caption: Stephen A. Smith, sports commentator and TV personality, speaks to reporters after meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House on November 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C.
Stephen A. Smith and President Donald Trump.

articles.title: Trump's top officials retreat behind military gates as ex-FBI deputy points to what's fueling threats
articles.summary: Scott Bessent joins Todd Blanche, Marco Rubio and Pete Hegseth at Washington D.C. military bases amid Iranian assassination threats.
articles.body:
Military bases around Washington, D.C., have become an increasingly common refuge for some of President Donald Trump's most powerful officials, as threats linked to Iran and a surge in threats against public officials raise security concerns across the administration.

"So you have this combination of a permission structure on the left for violence, combine it with the ability to track it and create a long paper trail, and the numbers explode, and these threat matrices go crazy," former Secret Service agent and former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest senior administration official to relocate to a military installation, joining a growing number of top Trump officials living behind military gates as federal authorities confront security threats that extend well beyond the White House.

"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the Secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the Secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety. The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials," a source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital.

Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats , a senior administration official told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, but did not elaborate.

The Iranian threats against Bessent come amid a documented history of alleged Tehran-backed assassination plots targeting senior U.S. officials.

Attorney General Todd Blanche also relocated to a military base from his home around March, a different source familiar with the arrangements told Fox News Digital on Thursday.

The Justice Department charged a member of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in 2022 in an alleged murder-for-hire plot targeting former Trump national security adviser John Bolton, while prosecutors disclosed in 2024 that another Iranian operative had allegedly been tasked with developing a plan to assassinate Trump.

Bongino said federal protection decisions are generally driven by threat assessments that account for threatening communications, social media activity and intelligence gathered by security personnel. Agencies responsible for protecting senior officials use those assessments to determine what level of protection is necessary.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran said last month that threats against the agency's full-time protectees had increased more than 40% from the previous year, with roughly 10,000 threat cases recorded in 2026 at the time.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Secret Service for comment.

"Pretty much, sadly, anyone at the cabinet, or even sub-cabinet level, with any kind of public persona in the Trump administration, needed a detail," Bongino said.

The assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and multiple attempts on President Donald Trump's life have heightened concerns about political violence, as security officials confront a growing volume of threats against public officials.

Bongino pointed to his own experience as FBI deputy director, saying his security needs were comparable to those of some of the government's highest-ranking law enforcement officials.

"Mine was on par with the attorney general and the FBI director that we had to expand it," Bongino said of his threat assessment and security detail. "It was an independent analysis."

Bongino said social media has made threats against public officials easier to track, but the sheer volume of online activity has also created more work for investigators trying to determine which threats are credible.

Bongino said the disruption to Bessent's personal life underscores the seriousness of the security concerns surrounding his move.

"For him to have to uproot his life. And move on to a military facility where the housing's not terrible in those places, but it's certainly not what he's used to," Bongino said. "This stuff, it's not a convenience issue, I can promise you that. This is definitely serious stuff."

Lawmakers have also raised concerns about security and federal spending. Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., secured House Armed Services Committee approval in June for a proposal seeking a Pentagon report on political appointees living in military housing, including the threats justifying their moves, legal authority for the arrangements and rental costs.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., also questioned whether the reported transfer of $415 million in Secret Service funding to White House construction projects could affect the agency's protective operations, citing federal watchdog concerns about staffing and resource shortages.

Barry Donadio, a former Secret Service agent who served during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, similarly told Fox News Digital that the decision to relocate Bessent to a military installation suggests an extraordinary level of concern among those responsible for his protection.

"My first inkling is that the [threat] is so high that they cannot protect him with certainty, unless he is on a military base which speaks volumes for the situation at hand," Donadio said.

Donadio said the move could indicate that officials believe Bessent would be safer on a military base than at a private residence.

"They may have foiled an attack already that is not being publicized, and as an extra measure, have moved him to a military base for protective custody," Donadio said, clarifying that he did not mean Bessent was in custody, but rather under heightened government protection.

Bessent is not the only senior Trump administration official whose security concerns have prompted a move to military housing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have reportedly taken up residence at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C., while White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing.

The relocations have not all stemmed from the same threats. Some followed concerns about domestic political violence, while Bessent's move comes amid reported threats linked to Iran.

Bongino said threats against high-profile officials can also extend beyond their time in government, describing an incident in which an individual allegedly appeared at a California television studio with a manifesto threatening him and other officials.

"I mean, this stuff is real, it happens every day," Bongino said. "And when you're living through it and you're not accustomed to it, you know, and it follows you after office too."

He said officials including Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Hegseth understood that public service in the administration could make them targets even after leaving office.

Fort McNair, a historic Army installation along the Potomac River in Washington, D.C., has emerged as one of the military properties housing senior Trump administration officials. The installation, which dates to the late 1700s, is home to the National Defense University and traditionally provides residential quarters for senior military leaders.

Fort McNair's residential quarters are divided into two housing groups, according to a 2020 National Capital Planning Commission report, while a 2024 Army filing identifies 27 historic homes built before 1919 at the installation.

The Army's housing website lists 88 historic dwelling units across Fort McNair and nearby Fort Myer combined, without specifying how many are at each base.

The growing use of military housing by senior civilian officials also raises questions about who approves the arrangements, whether officials pay for their accommodations and what impact, if any, the moves have on housing traditionally reserved for military personnel.

images.caption: Scott Bessent, US Treasury secretary, speaks to members of the media outside the White House in Washington, D.C., Nov. 5, 2025.

articles.title: Transportation secretary says he doesn’t apologize for FAA’s nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy declined to apologize for the nationwide ground stop that stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Sunday declined to apologize for the nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country following a router issue that derailed air traffic control communications.

Instead, the secretary blamed his predecessors and previous presidential administrations that he said did not do enough to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.

"It happened on my watch, but we have to be clear: I am moving at an incredible speed that no one has done at the FAA or in decades, and I'm proud of the work we're doing, the attention we're bringing to this issue," Duffy told NBC News' "Meet the Press." "But I can't apologize for what was passed off to us, and I can't blame Republicans or Democrats because it's all of them."

The secretary also blamed "30 years of a lack of investment," from the country's previous leaders.

"Why they didn't do that I don't know, but they gave me a system that needs to be fixed, and President [Donald] Trump and I are going to fix it," he added.

His remarks come less than two days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop that lasted several hours, leading to thousands of flight cancellations beginning on Friday and continuing through the weekend.

FAA contractor L3Harris was working on replacing a copper line with a fiber line at a remote site when the work led a router to overwhelm the national FAA telecommunications network, Duffy said Saturday.

Duffy also said Sunday on "Meet the Press" that he expects airports and airlines to resume normal operations by the end of the day or early Monday morning.

"By the end of today, into tomorrow, I think we'll be back to normal," he said, adding that Friday's ground stop led airplanes and flight crews to be "out of position."

"It takes some time for the airlines to rechoreograph all of their crews and aircraft. We're going to start seeing things get better today, but I think back to normal tomorrow," Duffy said.

The secretary also demurred when asked whether he could guarantee that a similar travel disruption won't happen in the future.

"First we have to figure out what happened. Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing their work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions. We don't want to shut down the airspace," Duffy told "Meet the Press" moderator Kristen Welker.

"We're going to figure out what was the root cause and then move forward from there, fixing how we do business at the FAA," he added.

Duffy also reiterated a call he's made all weekend for more funding from Congress to modernize the nationwide air traffic control system, which has long been outdated and faced problems.

"The president, since he came to office, has been pushing for modernization of the airspace. Before I was even sworn in, he brought this up," the secretary said, pointing to $12.5 billion that was allocated for air traffic control improvements in a GOP-backed spending bill last year.

"The Congress was very specific in how I spend that money. I have a certain allotment for radar, a certain allotment for radios, a certain allotment for building new infrastructure for my centers for air traffic controllers. They didn't give me money for telecom. They didn't give me money for new software," Duffy said.

"I'm coming back to Congress and the American people to explain all the great work we're doing right now," he continued. "We're going to spend that $12.5 billion by the end of 2028, but I need the rest of the money for software and a new telecom architecture that will be way more resilient. I need that money so I can start that build."

On Saturday, NBC News reported that on Thursday, just one day before the ground stop, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought sent a letter to members of Congress asking lawmakers for $30.1 billion to upgrade the United States' aging airports and air traffic control system.

They wrote: "This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure. These investments will address current challenges, including weather-related delays, while preparing the National Airspace System for emerging demands, such as safely integrating air traffic with the growing space industry."

On Sunday, Duffy urged Congress to "just do it."

"I'm doing all I can to keep people safe," he said. "But I'm also telling you, if you don't give us the resources, we can't complete the job. And this is — of all the partisanship — this is the most bipartisan thing in all of Washington. Democrats, Republicans, the president, everyone agrees on this. Let's just do it."

In a statement Sunday in response to questions about how the president plans to urge Congress to appropriate funds for the air traffic control infrastructure, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said, "The Trump administration immediately stepped into action at the first sign of issue to ensure the safety and security of all Americans. President Trump put the right leadership into place to effectively handle moments like these, and yesterday, all relevant leaders came together to coordinate a plan that put the safety of the American people first."

She added, "This administration will continue to monitor this situation and communicate to the American people through every necessary means."

images.caption: A stranded traveler sleeps Saturday in the terminal in Orlando, Fla. ( Christopher Beckett / NurPhoto via Getty)

articles.title: Trump blasts judge’s 2-week halt to his Washington golf project and says administration will appeal
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a “highly destructive and political decision” from a federal judge who ordered a two-week delay on...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a "highly destructive and political decision" from a federal judge who ordered a two-week delay on renovations at a historic Washington public golf course that he has been trying to redevelop into a championship-level venue.

In a social media post, Trump said his administration will "immediately appeal, on an expedited basis" the temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, which she issued just before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months.

"It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court," said Trump, who spent much of the weekend posting photos on his social media site of the golf course. "They don't call it Trash Island for no reason!"

Trump had announced work on the site along the Potomac River would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that the president's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something Trump has denied. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the judge's decision.

Reyes, in her ruling Saturday, noted that those posts presented a problem for the government, indicating that Trump's redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service "will close the Park to implement it."

Both points, she wrote, "favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

The order is in effect through Nov. 28. The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.

Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

articles.title: Luis Figo y Gabriel Rufián se enzarzan en X: "¡Lo que se hace por sobrevivir!" y "No todos nos vendemos"
articles.standfirst: El exfutbolista ha respondido con dureza al portavoz de ERC después de que ironizara sobre su posible nombramiento como ministro de Deportes en un Gobierno de PP y Vox
articles.summary: El exfutbolista ha respondido con dureza al portavoz de ERC después de que ironizara sobre su posible nombramiento como ministro de Deportes en un Gobierno de PP y Vox
articles.body: El político catalán Gabriel Rufián y el exfutbolista portugués Luis Figo han protagonizado un enfrentamiento en redes sociales después de que el portavoz de ERC en el Congreso de los Diputados bromeara sobre el posible futuro del exfutbolista en un hipotético Gobierno de coalición entre el Partido Popular y Vox. El intercambio de mensajes, que ha tenido lugar este domingo en X, antes Twitter, ha dejado varios reproches personales entre ambos. El origen de la polémica está en un mitin de Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya celebrado este viernes, en el que Gabriel Rufián, cabeza de lista de ERC a las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre, ironizó sobre los posibles nombramientos de un Ejecutivo formado por PP y Vox. Entre ellos, mencionó a Luis Figo como futuro ministro de Deportes. El comentario no ha pasado inadvertido para el exjugador del Real Madrid y del Barcelona, que este domingo ha decidido contestar directamente al político a través de su cuenta de X. Luis Figo le recuerda a Gabriel Rufián su pasado político En su publicación, Luis Figo ha respondido con un mensaje en el que cuestiona la trayectoria política del diputado y sus recientes movimientos para aglutinar a distintas formaciones de izquierdas. "¿Ya me echabas de menos? Bueno, cómo has acabado, chaval, de querer juntar a toda la izquierda a juntarte con Podemos. ¡Lo que se hace por sobrevivir!", ha escrito el exjugador. Luis Figo también ha aprovechado para recordar a Gabriel Rufián su candidatura a la alcaldía de Santa Coloma de Gramenet, en un mensaje en el que le acusa de vivir de la política: "Ya tienes una mala experiencia cuando fuiste candidato a la Alcaldía de Santa Coloma de Gramenet, ¿te acuerdas? Lo que se hace para vivir del cuento, pero ya no engañas a nadie. Suerte para el 29". La respuesta de Gabriel Rufián La contestación de Luis Figo ha tenido una rápida réplica por parte de Gabriel Rufián, que pocos minutos después ha publicado un mensaje en su perfil de X dirigido al exfutbolista. "No todos nos vendemos, as", ha escrito el político catalán, en una respuesta breve y contundente que parece aludir a la polémica que rodeó el fichaje del portugués por el Real Madrid en el año 2000, cuando abandonó el Barcelona para incorporarse al club blanco. De esta manera, el intercambio ha terminado, por el momento, con un nuevo reproche de Gabriel Rufián a Luis Figo, después de que la broma sobre su hipotético nombramiento como ministro de Deportes acabara convirtiéndose en un cruce de acusaciones personales en las redes sociales.

articles.title: As Trump administration implores Congress for additional FAA funding, Democrats say the agency already has it
articles.summary: Following a historic airspace meltdown on Friday that grounded all flights nationwide, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has implored Congress to authorize...
articles.body:
Following a historic airspace meltdown on Friday that grounded all flights nationwide, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has implored Congress to authorize tens of billions of dollars in additional funding for the Federal Aviation Administration.

But Democrats, who are set to take the majority in January, are pointing to legislation passed by Republicans last year that already gave the agency $12.5 billion, arguing that it already has the funds it needs.

"I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom. I can't build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s, but there's no money for that. There's no money for towers. Our towers are old," Duffy said on CNN's "State of the Union" with Dana Bash on Sunday.

Duffy had asked Congress for around $30 billion but after Friday's incident, he upped the request to $50 billion. President Donald Trump, in a social media post on Sunday, also urged Congress to "give the money, FAST!"

The transportation secretary said the ground stop was likely due to an issue that occurred while contractor L3Harris was switching an old copper wire at an air traffic location in El Dorado, Arkansas, to a more modern fiber optic system. It is unclear whether the outage was due to faulty equipment or contractor error.

Of the $12.5 billion given to the agency for three years under Trump's massive spending and policy bill — which no Democrats supported — $4.75 billion was allocated for "telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades." Duffy said at a news conference Saturday that the agency has spent about one-third of the modernization budget so far.

On Sunday, Duffy said all the telecom work can be done by "the first part of 2029."

"All I need is the money to finish it. And my, my hope is that if they give me money today, I'll be going tomorrow to build it," Duffy said.

Later Saturday, Reps. Rick Larsen and André Carson — the top Democrats on two House panels overseeing the aviation industry — asked the administration to explain to Congress why the agency needs more money if there are still unspent funds. The two added in a joint statement that FAA and DOT employees will brief their staff on Monday.

Meanwhile, some Democrats slammed the administration's priorities and how it has spent money in immigration enforcement and construction projects in Washington, DC, over aviation modernization and safety.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA," Hawaii Sen. Brian Schatz said in a post on X . "We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars."

Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth said in a post on X , "You've literally controlled Congress for the past two years. And apparently, there's always been money for vanity projects. But none to fix our air traffic control system? Perhaps Trump should prioritize aviation safety over his pathetic Arch."

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the House Appropriations Committee's top Democrat, called Duffy's $50 billion request a "ransom."

"Our air traffic controllers have been failed by Secretary Duffy," DeLauro said in a post on X, adding, "We need a competent partner at DOT."

However, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who launched a bid for Senate majority leader last week, signaled openness to supporting additional funds for the agency on Sunday while calling on administration officials to come to Congress and "justify" the ask.

"I will support whatever level of money is necessary to fix this problem. We should fix this problem on a bipartisan basis," Hollen told CNN on Sunday, but added, "It's really rich to hear the secretary pointing the fingers at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for. If they need more, they should come up and justify it."

Republicans could use the remaining weeks of their majority to approve additional funding for the agency, and outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson said Saturday that he would add FAA funding to an upcoming "legislative package."

"We don't really need any investigation to understand we need further investment," Johnson told Fox News. "We're going to work to get it done."

It was not immediately clear to congressional aides how leaders will pass new funding. Currently, appropriators are negotiating a government funding deal ahead of a December 11 deadline. Senate leadership aides in each party did not immediately respond to questions about the path forward in that chamber.

GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt is also pushing for passage of his bill, the Modern Skies Act , which would invest $30 billion in modernizing the nation's aviation system. The Missouri senator spoke with Trump on Friday, and has also spoken with Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on the topic.

CNN's Ellis Kim, Ted Barrett, Logan Schiciano, Isa Mudannayake and Aleena Fayaz contributed to this report.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: White House calls DC policies 'insanity' after 19-year-old gunman gets probation in shooting
articles.summary: A 19-year-old who prosecutors said fired more than 20 rounds into a D.C. neighborhood got probation, prompting the White House to slam the city's crime policies.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE – A 19-year-old who authorities say fired more than 20 rounds into a Washington, D.C., neighborhood and wounded a boy playing basketball has been released on probation, prompting the White House to denounce the city’s sentencing policies as "insanity." Prosecutors wanted Darius Drew behind bars for five years. Instead, a judge suspended a two-year prison sentence and ordered 18 months of supervised probation under the Youth Rehabilitation Act, a D.C. law U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro had previously urged lawmakers to overhaul. "The case illustrates the insanity of Washington, D.C.’s soft-on-crime policies that allow adults to receive just a slap on the wrist for dangerous crimes like firing twenty rounds of ammunition into the community," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS "It is remarkable that even with these types of radical policies in place, President Trump’s Safe and Beautiful Task Force has been able to drive down violent crime in our nation’s capital," Bis added. Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro granted Drew sentencing treatment under the Youth Rehabilitation Act over the government’s objection, according to federal prosecutors. Drew pleaded guilty Aug. 10 to aggravated assault and carrying a pistol without a license. CHAOTIC TEEN BRAWL GOES VIRAL AFTER TEEN TERROR PROMPTS US ATTORNEY PIRRO'S PLAN TO PROSECUTE PARENTS He was released Friday after spending nearly six months in custody following his May 22 arrest. Prosecutors opposed his release as well as the use of the youth sentencing law. The gunfire that put him there came from two locations in a Northwest Washington neighborhood, according to the government’s evidence. MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE On May 11, Drew rode a Lime bike into an alley before surveillance video captured him firing at a parked car, prosecutors said. The ShotSpotter gunfire detection system registered 10 shots. Seconds later, Drew fired toward a nearby house. A boy playing basketball at a recreation center was struck in the leg. By the time the shooting stopped, Drew had fired more than 20 rounds into the community, prosecutors said. Investigators later found two firearms, ammunition and large amounts of suspected narcotics and marijuana at his home. REPEAT OFFENDER ACCUSED OF SHOOTING NATIONAL GUARD MEMBER HAS LENGTHY HISTORY WITH THE LAW, RECORDS SHOW The probation ruling echoes a warning Pirro delivered to the D.C. Council more than a year earlier. In an Aug. 6, 2025, letter, she urged lawmakers to overhaul the Youth Rehabilitation Act, citing a separate case in which another 19-year-old received probation after shooting someone in the chest aboard a Metrobus. SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS The law, which the D.C. Council expanded in 2018, allows eligible offenders who committed crimes before turning 25 to receive sentences below otherwise applicable mandatory minimums and potentially have their convictions set aside, Pirro wrote. Murder and the most serious sexual abuse offenses are excluded. In that separate case described in the 2025 letter, the 19-year-old pleaded guilty to two offenses carrying five-year mandatory minimums but received probation after four months in jail awaiting trial, according to Pirro’s letter. SUSPECTED FLORIDA PUBLIX SLASHER WALKED FREE FROM COURT MONTHS EARLIER DESPITE VICTIM WARNINGS "This sentence was a legal sentence only because he was sentenced under the YRA," she wrote. Pirro argued the law needed changes to balance rehabilitation with accountability. Her office said 96% of defendants younger than 25 who received felony sentences in D.C. Superior Court from 2022 through 2024 were eligible for sentencing under the act. FBI REPORTS 114% JUMP IN VIOLENT CRIME ARRESTS UNDER TRUMP COMPARED TO BIDEN’S FINAL MONTHS The White House pointed to Trump’s Safe and Beautiful Task Force as its response to crime in the capital, saying the operation has made more than 19,000 arrests, including those of murderers, sex offenders, drug traffickers and other violent criminals. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the D.C. Council and Judge Di Toro’s office for comment.
